# Keḷisīlajātaka (Ja 202)
**ID:** Ja 202
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Keḷisīlajātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja202
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Keḷisīlajātaka* (Ja 202) is a birth story set at Jetavana, told by the Buddha concerning the elder monk Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. Although highly learned, sweet-voiced, and an arahant, Lakuṇṭaka was physically diminutive like a novice or dwarf; the Buddha related the tale to explain the mixed karmic fruits of his past deeds [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. Because it clarifies how previous actions yielded specific physical and spiritual results for a disciple in the present, the narrative functions like an *apadāna* [Appleton 2010].
In the story of the past, Lakuṇṭaka had been a king who delighted in mocking and pranking the elderly (*keḷisīla*), causing people to hide their elderly parents and causing filial piety to wither [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. Seeing fewer beings reborn in the heavenly realms, the Bodhisatta—who was then Sakka, king of the gods—manifested as a decrepit old man driving aged oxen in a broken wagon during a festival to teach and admonish the king to respect old age [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha reveals that the disrespectful king was Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya, while Sakka was the Bodhisatta [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1879]. In contemporary Sri Lankan Buddhist culture, the story is well known and depicted on decorative festival gateways (*toraṇa*) in Colombo at Vesak [Appleton 2010], while its opening verse (*Haṁsā koñcā mayūrā ti*) is included in modern anthologies of canonical verse [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral connect the text to discourses about the elder Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya in the *Bhikkhu Saṁyutta* (SN 21.6, *Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyasutta*) as well as two Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* discourses (SA 1063 and SA2 2) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms these connections computationally, showing high Pali-internal text reuse between Ja 202 (§0.4–2.4) and SN 21 (§6.2.1–6.3.4 with 0.99 similarity), along with automated alignments to the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99, fascicle 38) [DharmaNexus].
**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels (SuttaCentral): SN 21.6 Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyasutta; SA2 2 惡色; SA 1063 惡色
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Bhikkhu Saṁyutta (SN 21) (§0.4–2.4 ↔ §6.2.1–6.3.4)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): 雜阿含經 (ZH_T02_0099) [zh]
